opus-5.5.text:
I think the central challenge is that you're training two things at once that depend on each other: the experts and the router deciding which tokens go to which expert. That coupling causes most of the instability.

Early in training the router is essentially guessing. If a few experts get slightly more tokens by chance, they learn faster, become more useful, and attract even more tokens. That rich-get-richer loop produces load imbalance, and in the worst case expert collapse, where a handful of experts do all the work and the rest sit idle. You've paid for parameters you're not using.

The standard fix is an auxiliary load-balancing loss, but that brings its own tension. Push too hard on balance and you force tokens to experts that aren't the right fit, which hurts quality and blurs specialization. Push too softly and you get collapse. A lot of recent work, like bias-based balancing without an auxiliary loss, is really an attempt to get out of that trade-off.

The second piece is numerical. Router logits can drift large, and once they do, the softmax saturates, gradients get spiky, and you see loss spikes that are hard to recover from at scale. Techniques like router z-loss, careful precision for the gating computation, and conservative initialization exist because MoE is much less forgiving here than a dense model.

Then there's the systems side, which people tend to underestimate. Routing is dynamic, so the load on each device changes step to step. Capacity limits and token dropping interact with the learning dynamics, and communication across expert-parallel groups can turn small imbalances into real throughput and stability problems.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: the hard part is keeping the routing decisions sharp enough that experts actually specialize, while keeping them smooth and balanced enough that optimization doesn't fall apart. Most of the craft in training MoE well lives in managing that balance.

r001.rationale: The response describes uneven token routing across experts, the resulting load imbalance and expert collapse, and identifies keeping routing balanced as part of the central challenge. This conveys balancing experts’ activation rates.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When people ask about stability in MoE training, they usually expect me to say something about load balancing, and that is part of it, but I think the deeper issue is that you have introduced a discrete decision into an otherwise continuous optimization. The router picks a small number of experts for each token, and that choice is not differentiable in any clean way. So everything downstream of that choice is being trained on a path that can flip abruptly from one step to the next. That is the root of most of the pathologies we see.

Load imbalance is the most visible symptom. If a few experts start getting slightly more tokens, they get slightly more gradient, they get slightly better, and the router sends them even more. It is a rich-get-richer dynamic, and left alone it collapses the model into effectively a dense model with a lot of dead parameters. The standard remedy is an auxiliary balancing loss, but that is a blunt instrument. Push it too hard and you are forcing tokens onto experts that are bad for them, which hurts quality. Push it too little and collapse creeps back in. Tuning that coefficient across different scales is genuinely painful, and I do not think anyone has a principled answer yet.

The second thing, which gets less attention, is router logit growth. Over long training runs the router's outputs tend to drift to large magnitudes, the softmax saturates, and then a tiny perturbation in the logits can flip which expert wins. You see this as loss spikes that look random but are actually the router thrashing. Things like z-loss on the router or normalizing the gating inputs help a lot, and in my experience they matter more than people initially assume.

And then there is the systems side, which is inseparable from the algorithmic side. Capacity factors, token dropping, how you handle overflow when an expert is oversubscribed, all of those are engineering choices that change what the model actually sees during training. If you drop tokens inconsistently, you have introduced noise that interacts badly with the routing dynamics.

So if I had to summarize the central challenge in one sentence, it is that you are trying to learn a good discrete assignment and good experts at the same time, and each one destabilizes the other. Most of the tricks we have are ways of slowing that feedback loop down enough that both can converge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses load imbalance and auxiliary balancing loss, but identifies the central challenge as learning discrete assignments and experts together. It does not identify balancing expert activation probabilities as the central challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is that the router and the experts are learning at the same time, and each changes the other’s training conditions. The router decides which tokens an expert sees, while the expert’s performance influences what the router learns to send it. That feedback loop can amplify small imbalances: some experts get overloaded, while others receive too little training.

So you need to balance utilization without suppressing useful specialization. Perfectly uniform routing isn’t necessarily good routing. The goal is to let experts develop distinct capabilities while keeping token allocation, gradients, and routing decisions stable enough that all the experts continue to learn.

r001.rationale: The response says expert utilization and token allocation need to be balanced, describing the routing balance central to keeping MoE training stable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central challenge is the interaction between routing and expert learning. The router determines which tokens each expert sees, but the experts’ performance also influences how the router evolves. That creates a feedback loop: some experts can receive more tokens and improve faster, while others receive too few tokens to learn effectively.

So you need to balance utilization without preventing experts from specializing. And that balance needs to hold throughout training, not just on average. Stable training means keeping the router and the experts learning together, without letting either side reinforce an imbalance.

r001.rationale: The response says the router can send experts too many or too few tokens and that utilization must be balanced, which communicates balancing experts’ activation rates.
